items.text: One can refuse to judge another person's soul while still refusing absolutely to do what that person has done.
items.evidence: 'I have no window to look into another man's conscience. I condemn no one' — spoken in the same breath as 'No, I will not sign.'

items.text: Those who wrong us should be forgiven rather than cursed, even at the moment they destroy us.
items.evidence: To the executioner: 'I forgive you, right readily. Be not afraid of your office.' To Rich: 'I am sorrier for your perjury than my peril.'

items.text: Ambition tempts most sharply those who lack wealth and position, and small corruptions prepare the way for larger ones.
items.evidence: Rich sells the bribe cup, then perjures himself; Cromwell: 'There. That wasn't too painful, was it?... And you'll find it easier, next time.' More warns 'A man should go where he won't be tempted.'

items.text: Those who yield to coercion against their conscience deserve forgiveness rather than condemnation.
items.evidence: 'I have no window to look into another man's conscience. I condemn no one' — of those whose names are on the oath.

items.text: A person's private failings of anger and pride do not stay private; they extend outward into tyranny over those subject to them.
items.evidence: Henry's rage — 'They that say she is my wife are not only liars, but traitors!... See? You see how you've maddened me? I hardly know myself' — becomes the machinery that kills More.

items.text: A person who deceives others for personal gain is thereby a bad person.
items.evidence: Rich sells the bribe cup for a gown, spies for Cromwell, and perjures himself for the Attorney Generalship; the film's last line marks him as the one who escaped.

items.text: Private conscience rightly takes precedence over the commands of the state, even when disobedience is punishable by death.
items.evidence: More refuses the Oath knowing the penalty is death: 'I will not take the oath. I will not tell you why I will not,' and dies saying 'I die His Majesty's good servant but God's first.'

items.text: Remaining faithful to one's conscience is worth more than one's own life.
items.evidence: 'And if this be not enough to keep a man alive then in good faith, I long not to live.' The film's whole arc validates his refusal to purchase life by signing.

items.text: An oath binds the whole self, and cannot be honestly sworn while the heart silently dissents from it.
items.evidence: Meg proposes 'say the words of the oath and in your heart think otherwise'; More answers 'When a man takes an oath, he's holding his own self in his own hands like water... if he opens his fingers then, he needn't hope to find himself again.'

items.text: The forms and procedures of law deserve to be honoured even when they shelter wrongdoers, because they are also the innocent's only protection.
items.evidence: 'Go he should, if he were the Devil, until he broke the law'; 'And when the last law was down, and the Devil turned on you where would you hide, Roper, the laws all being flat?'

items.text: There is a spiritual order that precedes and outranks political authority, and rulers are bound by it.
items.evidence: 'The indictment is grounded in an act of parliament which is directly repugnant to the law of God and His Holy Church... the immunity of the Church is promised both in Magna Carta and in the King's own coronation oath.'

items.text: A person should hold to a moral conviction even when every institution, friend and loved one urges compromise.
items.evidence: Wolsey, Henry, Norfolk, Cranmer, Alice and Meg all press him to yield; 'The one fixed point in the world of turning friendship is that Sir More won't give in.'

items.text: When conscience or religious command conflicts with duty to one's country and its rulers, conscience rightly takes precedence.
items.evidence: 'I die His Majesty's good servant but God's first.'

items.text: Moral truth is fixed independently of what any authority declares it to be.
items.evidence: 'Some men think the earth is round, others think it flat... But if it is flat, will the King's command make it round?'

items.text: A person should avoid martyrdom by every honest means available, and accept it only when no honourable escape remains.
items.evidence: 'Our natural business lies in escaping... it's God's part, not our own, to bring ourselves to such a pass. If I can take this oath, I will.'

items.text: There are limits to political authority that no majority's consent can legitimately override.
items.evidence: Rich's testimony: 'Parliament had not the competence' to make the King Head of the Church, though it could dethrone him.

items.text: What most people have agreed to is a sufficient guide to what one ought to do.
items.evidence: Norfolk: 'look at these names. Why can't you do as I did, and come with us, for fellowship?' More: 'when we die... will you come with me, for fellowship?'

items.text: A person's highest loyalty is owed to their nation and its institutions, and private conviction should be set aside when the nation calls.
items.evidence: The Act of Supremacy is called 'repugnant to the law of God'; national institutions — Parliament, bishops, Convocation — all capitulate and are shown as capitulating.

items.text: There is an inviolable core of personal integrity that no power can take from a person.
items.evidence: 'I will not give in, because I oppose it. Not my pride, not my spleen... but I do, I. Is there... no sinew that serves no appetite of Norfolk's, but is just Norfolk?'

items.text: Careful adherence to law, together with prudent silence, can protect an honest person from a determined power.
items.evidence: More insists 'in silence is my safety, under the law' and 'there'll be no trial, they have no case' — yet Rich's perjury and a jury convicting without retiring destroy him.

items.text: Formal legal and institutional procedure is the proper instrument for establishing what happened and assigning guilt.
items.evidence: Cromwell instructs the jury need not retire; 'Guilty, my lord!' follows immediately on perjured testimony rewarded with the Attorney Generalship for Wales.

items.text: Private conscience is a higher court than either the law or the claims of one's family.
items.evidence: He defies both the King's law and his family's pleading: 'you have more regard for your own doubt than the King's command?' — 'For myself I have no doubt.'

items.text: Institutional authority is legitimate, but it must give way to an individual's protected conscience.
items.evidence: 'The King in parliament tells me that they are. Of course I recognize them' — he swears to the succession but not to the supremacy; 'I am the King's true subject.'

items.text: A sacred oath binds the conscience more effectively than the threat of legal penalty.
items.evidence: Henry 'will not give evidence... Because evidence is given on oath, and he will not perjure himself'; More: 'If what Master Rich has said is true I pray I may never see God in the face.'

items.text: Those who merely administer the decisions of power bear no real moral responsibility for what they help bring about.
items.evidence: Cromwell's self-description — 'our job as administrators is to minimize the inconvenience of things. That's our only job' — is placed against his manufacture of perjured evidence and his own later beheading.

items.text: When power demands the sincere assent of honest people rather than mere outward compliance, it shows that it doubts its own legitimacy.
items.evidence: Henry: 'Because you're honest. And what is more to the purpose, you're known to be honest'; Cromwell: 'This silence of his is bellowing up and down Europe.'

items.text: Standing on principle against overwhelming pressure is more often vanity than virtue.
items.evidence: Norfolk calls it 'disproportionate' and Alice 'this looks like cowardice,' but the film gives More the final speech and the dignified death, and Kate Cameron's praised 'steadfast refusal to kowtow to the king.'

items.text: Legal institutions can settle the moral substance of a dispute, and not merely its procedural form.
items.evidence: The trial establishes nothing true; the verdict is procured by Rich's false oath and Cromwell's direction of the jury.

items.text: Law and official procedure are the proper measure of what is right.
items.evidence: An act of parliament can be 'directly repugnant to the law of God'; 'It is therefore insufficient in law to charge any Christian to obey it.'

items.text: Acting in obedience to the law is by itself sufficient justification for what one does.
items.evidence: Cranmer's 'that you owe obedience to the King is not capable of question. So weigh a doubt against a certainty and sign' is refused, and the refusal is vindicated by the telling.

items.text: Obedience to lawful command is the highest duty of a person entrusted with a public task.
items.evidence: More resigns the Chancellorship rather than execute the King's policy: 'I have today resigned my office. I am no longer a great man.'

items.text: Refusing to lend one's gifts to an unjust power is a duty even when compliance would bring honour and belonging.
items.evidence: 'there is no honour which His Majesty would be likely to deny you' — refused; earlier, 'If you could come with me, there's no man I'd sooner raise.'

items.text: Silence in the face of unjust power is a betrayal even when the pressure to stay silent is overwhelming.
items.evidence: More's silence is treated as honourable and lawful: 'this was silence. And for my silence, I am punished with imprisonment'; 'The maxim of the law is, "Silence gives consent."'

items.text: Resistance to tyranny is worthwhile even when the resister is certain to be destroyed or replaced.
items.evidence: More cannot alter the Act or the marriage and knows it, yet 'we must stand fast a little even at the risk of being heroes'; the film honours the futile stand.

items.text: Keeping one's integrity may require departure and solitude rather than victory or reform from within.
items.evidence: More resigns and withdraws to Chelsea rather than serve the new order: 'I expect I'll write a bit... I think I'll learn to fish.'

items.text: Martial honour and high rank are reliable indicators of courage and integrity.
items.evidence: 'The nobility of England would have snored through the Sermon on the Mount. But you'll labour like scholars over a bulldog's pedigree'; 'You and your class have given in.'

items.text: Conformity to the group is a danger to be resisted, even at cost to one's standing.
items.evidence: The 'fellowship' exchange, and More alone opposing Wolsey: 'You were the only one.' 'Yes, Your Grace.'

items.text: An obscure life of useful service is a lesser calling than a life of public influence and renown.
items.evidence: Rich: 'If I was [a great teacher], who would know it?' More: 'You! Your pupils. Your friends. God. Not a bad public, that.'

items.text: Standing firm on principle is compatible with loving one's family well; integrity need not wound those closest to us.
items.evidence: Alice: 'I'll tell you what I'm afraid of that when you've gone, I shall hate you for it'; the household is dismissed and the family reduced to cutting greens for fuel.

items.text: Devotion to a cause larger than oneself should take precedence over private attachments.
items.evidence: 'Finally, it isn't a matter of reason. Finally, it's a matter of love' — and he orders the family abroad: 'Alice, I command you!'

items.text: A friendship should rightly be given up when continuing it would put the friend in danger.
items.evidence: 'No one is safe, Howard, and you have a son. We'll end our friendship now.' — 'For friendship's sake?' — 'Yes.' He then stages a quarrel to drive Norfolk off.

items.text: Vows and confidences create real obligations, and betraying them is the paradigmatic wrong.
items.evidence: Rich's sworn perjury is the hinge of the film: 'In good faith, Rich, I am sorrier for your perjury than my peril.'

items.text: Political conviction should follow whichever power is currently ascendant.
items.evidence: Rich's ascent by attaching himself to Cromwell and the King is framed as the loss of innocence: 'I was lamenting. I've lost my innocence.'

items.text: Doing what is right carries real costs that its goodness does not cancel, and the innocent still suffer.
items.evidence: 'We don't read because we've no candles. We don't talk because we wonder what they're doing to you' — More's rightness does not cancel his family's ruin, and he is executed anyway.

items.text: Worldly fortune tracks moral desert: the wicked come to bad ends and the good are vindicated within this life.
items.evidence: More is beheaded and his head stuck on Traitor's Gate; Rich prospers to the Chancellorship and dies in bed.

items.text: Doing what is right generally brings the doer some form of reward or relief.
items.evidence: More's rightness yields poverty, the Tower and the block; no relief follows in this life.

items.text: Wrongdoers are ultimately caught and made to answer for what they have done.
items.evidence: Epilogue pointedly ends: 'Richard Rich became Chancellor of England and died in his bed,' the perjurer alone escaping the reckoning.

items.text: Persistent effort and moral determination are eventually rewarded with a just outcome.
items.evidence: More's meticulous legal determination — 'I like to keep my affairs regular' — cannot produce a just outcome against a directed court.

items.text: The appetite for power corrupts those who pursue it and destroys the affections that compete with it.
items.evidence: Rich's pursuit of place costs him his friendship and his oath; 'it profits a man nothing to give his soul for the whole world. But for Wales.'

items.text: The exact wording of what is said carries moral weight, and an inaccurate rendering of another's words can do as much harm as a deliberately hostile act.
items.evidence: 'Tell me the words. An oath is made of words. It may be possible to take it'; and Rich's rendering corrected — 'Parliament had not the competence.' 'Or words to that effect.'

layers.content:
## Plot
The film covers the years 1529 to 1535, during the reign of Henry VIII.
During a private late-night meeting at Hampton Court, Cardinal Wolsey, Lord Chancellor of England, chastises More for being the only member of the privy council to oppose Wolsey's attempts to obtain from the Pope an annulment of Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, as their marriage has not produced a male heir. With the annulment, Henry would be able to marry Anne Boleyn, with whom he hopes to father such an heir and avoid a repeat of the Wars of the Roses. More says that he cannot agree to Wolsey's suggestion that they apply "pressure" on Church property and revenue in England. Unbeknownst to More, the conversation is being overheard by Wolsey's ambitious aide, Thomas Cromwell.
Returning to his home at Chelsea at dawn, More finds his young acquaintance Richard Rich waiting for his return to lobby for a position at Court. More instead offers Rich a job as a teacher. Rich declines More's offer, saying that teaching would offer him little chance to become well known. More finds his daughter Meg chatting with a brilliant young lawyer, William Roper, who announces his desire to marry her. The devout Catholic More says he cannot give his blessing as long as Roper remains a Lutheran, who are considered members of the heretical Protestant movement.
Wolsey is dismissed from office when the annulment is not granted and dies in disgrace in a rural monastery, with More succeeding him as Lord Chancellor. The King makes an "impromptu" visit to the More estate and again requests More's support for an annulment. Still, More remains unmoved as Henry alternates between threats, tantrums, and promises of unbounded royal favors. Cromwell, now the King's Principal Secretary, bribes Rich with the promise of a position at Court if he will spy on More.
Roper, learning of More's quarrel with the king, says that his religious views have altered considerably and declares that by attacking the Church, the king has become "the Devil's minister." More admonishes Roper to be more guarded when Rich again pleads for More to grant him an office. When More again refuses, Rich denounces More's steward as a spy for Cromwell. An unmoved More responds, "Of course, that's one of my servants." Humiliated, Rich ends his friendship with More.
Meanwhile, the king orders Parliament and the bishops to declare him "Supreme Head of the Church of England". Embracing Caesaropapism, the bishops and Parliament accede to the king's demands and renounce all allegiance to the Pope. More quietly resigns as Lord Chancellor rather than accept the new order. His close friend and successor, Thomas Howard, attempts to draw out his opinions in a friendly private chat, but More knows that the time for speaking openly of such matters is over.
In a meeting with Norfolk, Cromwell implies that More's troubles will be over if he attends the king's wedding to Boleyn. After More does not, he is summoned again to Hampton Court and interrogated mercilessly by Cromwell. More refuses to answer any questions, and an infuriated Cromwell sends him away. The Thames boatmen are aware of the King's hostility to More and refuse to ferry him, so More returns home on foot.
As More finally arrives, his daughter Meg informs him that a new oath is being circulated and that all must take it or face charges of high treason. Initially, More says he might be willing to take the oath, depending on its wording. Upon learning that it names the king as head of the Church, legitimizes his Lutheran heirs, and allows no legal or moral loopholes, More refuses to take it and is imprisoned in the Tower of London.
At an inquiry chaired by Cromwell and Norfolk, More remains steadfast in his refusal to take the Oath and refuses to explain, knowing that he cannot be convicted if he has not explicitly denied the king's supremacy. Cromwell punishes More by confiscating his prized collection of books. As Rich collects the books, he and his former friend share a final debate over More's choices. More says goodbye to his wife Alice, Meg, and Roper, urging them not to try to defend him, but to leave the country.
At his trial, More refuses to express an opinion about the king's second marriage or why he will not take the Oath, based upon the legal principle that silence is to be interpreted as consent. Cromwell calls Rich to testify. Rich alleges that, when he went to confiscate More's books, More told him that while Parliament has the power to dethrone the king, it does not have the authority to make the king the Head of the Church.
A horrified More offers to take any oath required by the court that he never said any such thing to Rich. More adds that he would never be so suicidal as to entrust so dangerous an opinion "to such a man as that." As Rich leaves the witness box, it emerges that Rich has been made Attorney General for Wales as a reward from Cromwell for committing perjury, much to More's chagrin.
Under a direct order from Cromwell, the jury convicts More without leaving the courtroom to deliberate. But as the judges begin to pronounce the death penalty, More interrupts and reminds them that prisoners are to be asked before sentencing if they have anything to say.
Upon being so asked by the judges, More declares that he does. More calls Parliament's Act of Supremacy repugnant to every legal precedent and institution in all the history of Christendom. He cites the Biblical foundation for the Petrine Primacy and the authority of the Papacy, rather than national governments, over the Church. Furthermore, he declares that the Church's freedom from state control and interference is guaranteed both in the Magna Carta and in the king's own coronation oath. As uproar ensues, the judges sentence More to death by beheading.
The scene switches from the court to Tower Hill on July 6th, 1535, where More observes custom by pardoning and tipping the executioner. More declares, "I die his Majesty's good servant, but God's first." He kneels at the block and, off-screen, the executioner cuts off More's head.
In the epilogue, a narrator describes the aftermath and the fates of those involved in More's downfall, with Thomas Cromwell himself beheaded for treason five years later, Archbishop Cranmer being burned at the stake, and Norfolk narrowly avoiding his own execution due to Henry's death from syphilis. The only exception is Richard Rich, who "became Chancellor of England, and died in his bed."

layers.label: Critical reception
layers.content:
## Reception > Critical Reception
A Man for All Seasons received positive reviews from film critics, with an 89% "Fresh" rating on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes and an average rating of 7.70/10, based on 82 reviews. The critics' consensus states: "Solid cinematography and enjoyable performances from Paul Scofield and Robert Shaw add a spark to this deliberately paced adaptation of the Robert Bolt play." On Metacritic, the film holds a weighted average score of 72 out of 100 based on 11 critics, indicating "generally favorable reviews". A. D. Murphy of Variety wrote: "Producer-director Fred Zinnemann has blended all filmmaking elements into an excellent, handsome and stirring film version of A Man for All Seasons."
Scofield's performance was particularly praised. Kate Cameron of the New York Daily News wrote, "over all these fine performances, including Robert Shaw's opulent, bluff and forceful representation of the king, it is Scofield who dominates the screen with his genteel voice and steadfast refusal to kowtow to the king, even at the expense of his head." Pauline Kael gave the film a more critical review, writing, "There's more than a little of the school pageant in the rhythm of the movie: Though it's neater than our school drama coaches could make it, the figures group and say their assigned lines and move on."
In 1995, on the occasion of the 100th anniversary of cinema, the Vatican included it among its list of important films. In 1999, British Film Institute named A Man for All Seasons the 43rd greatest British film of all time. In 2008, it came 106th on Empire magazine's 500 Greatest Movies of All Time list.
